To check (7)

To check Ethics Approval Check

What we found

1 of 1 paper appeared to report data about people or animals that need an ethics statement, and lacked one.

Show details

The paper appears to report data that the authors collected from people or animals, but we found no ethics statement. Such data need one: approval by an ethics committee, or a reason why none was needed. We based this on the sentences below. A paper can describe someone else’s study in the same words; if these data are not the authors’ own, no statement is needed.

We based this on:

In total 21 participants (11 males and 10 females) were recruited via Sussex SONA participant pool, in exchange for credits, ages ranged from 19 to 35 years, with an average of 24.52 years.

The SONA advertisement instructed participants to wear glasses (or contact lenses) to the experiment if they had any eyesight refractive problems (myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism), and that people with a squint (strabismus) were excluded.

In the rating of attractiveness, participants were instructed to rate every image on a 5-point Likert Scale, ranging from “5 -aroused”, “4 -intrigued” to “3 -indifferent”, “2 -repelled” and “1 -disgusted”.

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 1 non-significant p value that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .664 The invalid pattern criterion excluded another 55 participants from the subliminality analysis, which showed a chance-level performance (M = .50, SD = .02), t(54) = -0.44, p = .664, BHC(0, .07 proportion correct units) = 0.018 RRB<1/3 [.003, >.50].

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

We found no codebook or README documentation for the 75991 extracted data columns.

README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including ‘README’ in the name of your overview document.

Study/Repository Mismatch

The studies named in the manuscript do not match how the repository’s files are grouped: the repository separates out studies (ex2, pilot1) not named in the manuscript. Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.

File Naming

File names should be machine-parseable: no spaces or special characters, and every file should be classifiable by name or extension. We found 13 naming problems that should be fixed, and 10 files with a naming suggestion (not required, but a good habit).

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 2 code files.

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 5 distinct packages/libraries: bayesplay, dplyr, kableExtra, papaja, scales. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

To check Data Check

What we found

  • We classified 303 files: 197 data, 6 code, 9 documentation, 91 materials.
  • We found 197 tabular data files and extracted 75991 columns from 197 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 3 study groups (ex1, ex2, pilot1), plus 2 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata). We ran automated data-quality checks on 75991 columns; 238 columns have at least one potential issue (189 columns whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long; 40 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 12 columns whose name suggests personal information; 6 columns that look like geographic coordinates; 3 columns whose values look like personal information). 3 files are a Qualtrics survey export. 194 of 197 spreadsheet files have at least one formatting issue (colour coding, merged cells, empty rows/columns, or an offset header).
Show details

This module classifies repository files and, for tabular data files available locally, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 75991 columns across 2922 data files.

Issues Identified

3524 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 2922 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 4 R code files.

Run order

A dependency cycle was detected among 2 files (pilot_study_files/analysis_report.qmd, main_study_files/analysis_report.qmd): each reads a file another writes, so no run order satisfies all of them. This must be resolved before the code can run.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 pilot_study_files/helper_functions.R — none
2 main_study_files/helper_functions.R — none

File paths

The data paths in the code to files the repository holds work as deposited, but 1 path names a file the repository does not hold: combined_data.xlsx.

Files not run on their own

2 files only define functions, so running them on their own says nothing: a function counts when a script uses it. These files are not counted as scripts. 0 are used by no script in the deposit.

File Used by
pilot_study_files/helper_functions.R pilot_study_files/analysis_report.qmd, main_study_files/analysis_report.qmd, main_study_files/helper_functions.R
main_study_files/helper_functions.R pilot_study_files/helper_functions.R, pilot_study_files/analysis_report.qmd, main_study_files/analysis_report.qmd

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 2 were run by another script with source(). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 2 scripts were not started, or stopped early, because the time for all scripts together had run out. The checks before this one had left 0 sec before the time limit, too little to copy the repository, install its packages and run its scripts (at least 15 min), so none of that was done.

Calls that install packages in the code

2 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

Run by another script

2 scripts are run by another script with source(), so they were not run on their own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on their own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Their outcome is part of the sourcing script’s outcome.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
