Discussion

The pilot aimed to replicate the procedure of Jiang et al. (2006), as closely as possible using CFS. In terms of the first manipulation check, the subliminality of the nude images, there was evidence that subjects were above chance in discriminating the side of the naked image, and hence above the objective threshold. The proportion correct may also be an underestimate. Four of 21 total participants engaged in

Heterosexual Females (N=8) Heterosexual Males (N=7) Mdiff SE t p B RR Mdiff SE t p B RR F images (UnCon) *.06 .04 1.36 .217 0.23 [.064, >1] -.02 .03 -0.6 .571 0.19 [.054, >1] M images (UnCon) .01 .03 0.22 .833 0.38 [<.001, .116]** *.03 .03 0.77 .472 0.22 [.062, >1] F images (Con) *.02 .02 1.21 .265 0.11 [.03, >1] -.06 .04 -1.6 .162 0.21 [.058, >1] M images (Con) .01 .03 0.34 .747 0.44 [<.001, .137]** *-.01 .03 -0.29 .778 0.38 [<.001, .115]** stereotyped responses, defined operationally as more than 20% of the trials (i.e. 16) in a row eliciting the same left/right response.

In analysing priming in the pilot, we removed trials from the unconscious condition where participants indicated they saw the image. Post hoc selection of trials can lead to regression to the mean effects (Shanks, 2017), whereby the true proportion of in reality seen trials, in a subset nominally selected to be unseen trials, is best estimated by a mean closer to that in the total of all trials (i.e. the proportion of in reality seen trials is not zero in that subset of trials selected as nominally unseen). The effect arises because of noise in the measurement of whether a trial is seen or unseen. Thus, the priming effect of the nominally unseen trials may be the priming contributed by contamination from in-reality-seen trials. Given Jiang et al. (2006) claim that conscious trials do not lead to priming, only unconscious trials do, then regression to the mean could not be the explanation for any unconscious priming obtained. However, considering the small sample size, the pilot did not provide sufficient evidence to either support or reject Jiang's conclusion regarding the existence of priming in the conscious condition. Their conclusion was based on the non-significant priming effects in the conscious condition, which is insufficient grounds to accept the null hypothesis.

However, according to the supplementary material from Skora et al. (2023), the contamination of conscious data may only become a threat when it's more than 20%, unless performance on conscious trials is large. As a precautionary measure, the procedure for determining whether the proportion correct in the unconscious trials exceeds what could maximally be produced by regression to the mean (i.e. contamination by conscious perception) used by Dienes (2022), Jurchis and Dienes (2023), and Skora et al. (2023), will be employed in the main experiment. The procedure estimates the maximum contamination there could be in order to provide an upper limit on what priming could be in the unconscious condition, given no priming effect in genuine unconscious trials, combined with a contribution to priming by those conscious trials mismeasured as unconscious. This enables an interval H0 for priming in the unconscious condition to be used, with the upper limit of the null interval being the most priming could be, given contamination by conscious trials. This brief explanation is spelt out in detail, with the relevant equations described, in Dienes (2022), and Skora et al. (2023; Supplementary materials).

The interval (rather than point) model of H0 will be used in the Bayes factor for testing priming effects.

There was largely insensitive evidence supporting the claim that there is no conscious priming by nude images in CFS. Also using CFS, Lapate et al. (2014) found participants' emotional responses (measured with SCRs) were significantly related to their subjective evaluations of neutral faces only when the priming from emotional faces was unconscious, despite SCRs being observed in both conditions. One possibility for the Jiang et al. paradigm is that attention is moved more quickly in the conscious versus unconscious condition and had already returned to centre by the time the Gabor patch came to be judged (maybe especially in participants who believe they should not be staring at naked bodies in lab conditions). That is, the timings of the paradigm may have become optimized for unconscious but not conscious conditions.

In terms of the second manipulation check (not included in Jiang et al.) that the nude images picked for the experiments are attractive or unattractive to participants, as appropriate, there was evidence this check was passed for heterosexual males, but the evidence was inconclusive for females. The wording used in the rating scale could be responsible for this inconclusive result. Ratings such as "aroused" and "disgusted" might be too extreme for participants to choose in a laboratory setting with a glimpse of the images. We will change the scale for the main experiment. While the images may turn out not to pass this check, as we are attempting to replicate Jiang et al. (2006) as closely as we can, a failure to pass this check in the main experiment will be an interesting fact concerning the paradigm, at least as applied to UK participants in the 2020s.

Testing the theory regarding an individual's homophobic tendency, the participants universally possessed positive explicit attitudes toward different sexual orientations.

Developed countries' societal attitudes toward LGBTQ have progressed over the past few decades, especially among the younger generation (Ayoub & Garretson, 2017; Siva Ilango et al., 2020). Though the UK society is definitely not "homophobic-free", it seems unlikely we will gather enough high-homophobic participants for analysis with any reasonably sized sample of Sussex students. Social expectation bias might be another factor at play. Despite guaranteed anonymity, homophobic participants might suppress their genuine attitudes. Thus, we will not pre-register any hypothesis concerning this prediction, but keep the scale in for exploration.

Concerning the main theory to be tested, of subliminal attentional effects from nude images, the data were not evidential either way -an expected outcome. But now we are in a position to estimate the required sample size. The lack of convincing evidence with the current sample size does have an immediate important practical implication: With the number of trials used, the procedure is far too noisy to be used as a surreptitious sexuality detector for a single individual. An order of magnitude more trials would be needed in principle.

The level of discrimination accuracy with the current version of Gabor patches also requires attention. CFS participants, on average, performed at 82.5% accuracy (SD = .12), with five participants hitting 100% accuracy in some conditions. The current parameters of the Gabor patches might not be the most optimal. That is, there may be a ceiling effect so that attention cannot improve performance by much. Ideally, we should keep performance on the patches around 60-80% with no priming. We will shift subjects towards this region by an initial staircasing in the practice trials on the contrast of Gabor patches.

We also noticed a difference in our stimuli and those of Jiang et al. (2006). Their scrambled images had a rectangular shape (see their Figure 1); our scrambled images had a body outline (see our Given the difficulty of recruiting non-heterosexual participants, we will make predictions and ensure sensitivity only for heterosexual participants, while running any other participant who turns up for exploratory analyses.

Main Study

We now present the predictions we test, and the theories they bear on. On the theory that the CFS constrained seeing which side the naked images were at the objective threshold, subjects should be at chance at indicating which side the naked image was. On the theory that the CFS rendered knowledge of the side subliminal, then even if subjects are above the objective threshold, they should be at the subjective threshold in indicating which side the image was on.

On the theory that the images are actually attractive to subjects according to their sexuality, subjective ratings of the attractiveness of the images should follow sexual preferences, with, in particular, heterosexual people finding opposite sex images sexually attractive and same sex images sexually unattractive. (We do not guarantee we will collect enough data for homosexual participants.)

On the theory that conscious perception allows the attentional shift to be overcome by the time the Gabor patch is to be judged, there should be no conscious priming.

Given these manipulation checks are passed, we can test the main hypothesis. On the theory that attention can be drawn to subliminal images of the sex preferred by one's sexuality, attentional priming should be above chance for each heterosexual males and females for the images of the opposite sex. Given the greater consistency of the attraction rather than the repulsion effect in Jiang et al., we will only guarantee enough data for the attraction effect.

Method

Participants. We estimated the needed sample size for each of the predictions. We set the threshold for the stopping rule to 5 and 1/5 to ensure the robustness of the decision threshold (a B > 3 or < 1/3).

The SD of the proportion of correct answers for the nude image location discrimination task for unconscious and conscious trials was .12 and .03 (N = 10), respectively. The 95% CI on the ratio of the corresponding variances (SD squared) was [5.23, 84.72]. For testing discrimination for unconscious trials, the SD of .12 was divided by √N and used as the SE in a Bayes factor calculator for a half-Cauchy model with a mode of 0 and scale factor of .5/7 = .07 (this follows from the maximum proportion correct can be above chance = 0.5; and the rough maximum plausible value for a Cauchy can be taken to be scale factor×7: Dienes, 2019). Assuming a .07 proportion difference in proportion of correct for H1 and 0 for H0, an N of 16 was required to find B > 5 and an N of 12 for a B > 3 if H1 were true (and the sample mean difference was .07), and an N of 49 was required to find B < 1/5 and an N of 15 for a B <1/3 if H0 were true and the sample mean difference was 0. We ran until the stopping rule was reached, that was until Bayes factors for the proportion of correct from unconscious trials reached the lower (1/5) or higher (5) threshold for each of male and female participants, or a maximum N of 100 was reached.

Using a fully informed scale factor would be better than the above method: Dienes (2015) recommended using the priming found in the conscious condition as a way of estimating what discrimination performance would be needed in the nominal unconscious condition in order for it to explain priming. While the latter method better motivates the model of H1, if there is no priming in the conscious condition (as Jiang et al. 2006 claim), this method cannot be used. However, there may be conscious priming. Thus, if we obtain evidence for conscious priming, then we will use the method of Dienes (2015) to ensure that the test of objective awareness in the unconscious condition is appropriate, we will estimate the level of objective performance expected given the amount of "unconscious" priming, assuming the same ratio of discrimination performance above chance to priming as in the conscious condition. A possible problem is that this method assumes a linear relation between priming and discrimination task performance, which may not be reasonable over a large range. Thus, if the estimate is larger than .07, we will revert to the .07 estimate so as not to bias evidence in favour of H0. This estimate will be used as the SD of a halfnormal in the model of H1.

For the ratings of attractiveness, the SD of expected attractive and repulsive ratings was .71 and .47, respectively, for all participants whose sexuality allowed a clear prediction of attraction and repulsion (N = 18). Treating the population error variance as the same in all cases, yields a rough overall estimate of the SD of the subjective ratings of √((.71 2 + .47 2 )/2) = .60. This was divided by √N and used as the SE in a Bayes factor calculator, assuming a .5 difference in attractiveness ratings for H1 and 0 for H0, until the Bayes factor threshold was reached (Dienes, 2015), an N of 8 was required to find B > 5 and an N of 6 for a B >3 if H1 were true (and the sample mean were .5), an N of 35 was required to find B < 1/5, and an N of 13 for a B < 1/3 if H0 were true (and the sample mean were 0). Thus, we ran until the stopping rule was reached, that was until Bayes factors for subjective attractive or repelling ratings reached the lower (1/5) or higher (5) threshold separately for male and female participants, or a maximum N of 100 was reached.

For the priming effect, the SD of attraction and repulsion for unconscious trials was .08 and .11, respectively, for all participants whose sexuality allowed a clear prediction of attraction and repulsion (N = 15), and .11 and .07 for the conscious trials (N = 15). The 95% CI on the ratio of variances was [0.21, 1.88] for the unconscious condition, and [0.81, 7.20] for the conscious condition. For simplicity, treating the population error variance as the same in all cases, yields a rough overall estimate of the SD of the priming effect of √((.08 2 + .11 2 + .11 2 + .07 2 )/4) = .09. This was divided by √N and used as the SE in a Bayes factor calculator, assuming a .10 priming of proportion correct for H1 gathered from Jiang et al. (2006) and 0 for H0. An N of 21 was required to find B < 1/5 and an N of 8 for a B < 1/3 if H0 were true (and the sample mean was 0), an N of 6 was required to find B > 5 and an N of 4 for a B > 3 if H1 were true (and the sample mean was 0.1). We ran until the stopping rule was reached namely, for the B on the attraction priming effect to reach the lower (1/5) or higher (5) threshold separately for male and female participants, or a maximum N of 100 was reached.

For the absence of a priming effect in conscious trials, the SD of attraction and repulsion for conscious trials was .11 and .07 (N = 15). Treating the population error variance as the same in all cases yields a rough overall estimate of the SD of the priming effect of √((.11 + .07)/2) = .09. As for the estimation for the priming effect, this was divided by √N and used as the SE in a Bayes factor calculator, assuming a .10 priming of proportion correct for H1 and 0 for H0, until the Bayes factor threshold was reached.

An N of 19 was required to find B < 1/5 and an N of 7 for a B < 1/3 if H0 were true, and an N of 5 was required to find B > 5 and an N of 4 for a B > 3 if H1 were true. We ran until the stopping rule was reached for all pre-registered tests, in this case, until Bayes factors for a conscious priming effect reached the lower (1/5) or higher (5) threshold separately for male and female participants or a maximum N of 100 was reached.

Procedure

The same procedure as the pilot was used with the following exceptions.

To prevent participants from giving stereotyped responses in the direct test, further instructions were provided at the start of each test. Participants were told: "Please make a guess even if you do not see anything. Go by what you thought you might have seen, even weakly, on each trial, without deciding in advance what your response will be.

The correct answer will be left or right randomly; thus, say left or right about equally often, without deciding on any pattern for your answers in advance".

For measuring subjective attractiveness, the options were changed to be less extreme. The survey was a 5-point Likert scale with the question, "How personally sexually attractive to you is this image?". For the ratings, we used "indifferent" as the centre point 0, "very unattractive" as -2, "moderately unattractive" as -1, "moderately attractive" as 1, and "very attractive" as 2. This should keep participants' responses within the "subjective attractiveness" concept, corresponding to the attentional effects we aimed for.

To tackle the ceiling effect observed in participants' proportion of accuracy in identifying the Gabor patches, the main study adapted the staircase measure to customise the contrast of Gabor patches for each participant. The Gabor patch staircase was employed after the practice trials. The staircase worked as a round of 10 trials, with

Gabor patches (tilted 1° clockwise or counterclockwise) randomly appearing on the left or right to the centre focus cross for 100ms each time, followed by an orientation identification task. To mimic the attention shift proposed in Jiang et al. (2006), an arrow appeared for 300ms in the centre of participants' eyesight, indicating the location the Gabor patch would be. The proportion of accuracy for these 10 trials would be the reference for staircasing. If the participant's accuracy was higher than 80%, the procedure would start over with the Gabor patches reduced in contrast by 10%. If the participant performs worse than 60%, the contrast for the Gabor patches will be increased by 5% for the next round. Once the participant's performance falls into the 80-60% interval, another round of trials would proceed with the same contrast to ensure the accuracy of the result. If the second round's performance still met the threshold, the staircasing ends.

Other minor adjustments included a change of wording in the confidence check (from "somewhat confident" to "some confidence") to imply any confidence is relevant.

The confidence check for the Gabor patch identification task was removed since it is not crucial to the research questions (see Figure 2).

Analysis.

For each prediction, we specified the test of that prediction. As for the pilot, Bayes factors (B) were used to represent the strength of the evidence supporting the alternative hypothesis (H1) compared to the null hypothesis (H0). A threshold of 3 and 1/3 will be used for drawing conclusions from Bayes factors. By convention, a B between roughly 3 and 10 is moderate evidence for H1, and a B over 10 is strong evidence; similarly, for evidence for H0, the rough threshold of moderate and strong evidence is 1/3 and 1/10 respectively.

For the prediction of subliminality, the proportion of correct discrimination of the side of intact nude images in the direct test was used to determine whether perception is at the objective threshold. If conscious priming is not found, the model of H1 will be the probability distribution of a half-Cauchy, with a mode of 0 and a scale factor of 0.5/7 = .07 proportion correct above 0.5. If conscious priming is found for a given gender, the method of Dienes (2015) would be used to determine an expected discrimination performance, and if this is less than .07 it will instead be used as the SD of a half-normal.

For the prediction of subjective attractiveness, the model of H1 was a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and an SD of 0.5 Likert units. We tested male and female heterosexual participants separately for the attractiveness of nude images of their opposite sex.

For the prediction of attentional effects, the proportion of difference in performance of accuracy in the Gabor patch identification task was tested. Using Jiang et al. (2006) to inform the roughly expected effect size, the model of H1 was a halfnormal distribution with a mean of 0 and an SD of 0.1 proportion correct units. H0 was modelled by a uniform distribution going from 0 to a maximum defined by the highest priming that could be produced by contamination by conscious trials, as per the procedure given in the supplementary materials of Skora et al. (2023). (Note we did not use this procedure in the pilot, because we did not find evidence for conscious priming.)

We tested for heterosexual participants' subliminal attention being attracted to the location of nude images of their opposite sex with a separate test for men and women for the unconscious trials.

Exclusions. For the attentional task, trials were excluded from the unconscious condition if participants indicated they saw the image, and whole participants excluded for reporting seeing the naked image on more than 20% of unconscious trials. Whole participants were excluded if on the awareness discrimination task when they used the same "left" or "right" response more than 16 trials in a row at any point in the test, which suggests they lose task engagement, or reported they saw the naked image on more than 20% of unconscious trials.

Pre-registered Results

The final sample, satisfying the stopping rule, was 173 participants with ages ranging from 18 to 53 years, with an average of 20.98 years (SD = 5.36). There were 63 heterosexual females, 37 heterosexual males, 50 bisexual females, five bisexual males, 16 homosexual females, and two homosexual males.

Complete data for these analyses are at OSF osf.io/82xua.

Subliminality of the images.

For this stage of analysis, a total of 70 participants were excluded (as per pre-registered exclusion criteria), with 15 exceeding the breakthrough threshold and the remaining 55 delivering invalid responses, leaving 103 participants. Among participants excluded for invalid response patterns, on average, 115.74 of 160 unconscious trials were delivered with a consecutive response. The proportion correct discrimination of the side of the intact image in unconscious trials was (M = .53, SD = .09), t(102) = 3.64, p<.001, BHC(0, .07 proportion correct units) = 92.4 RRB>3 [<.001, >.5]; and for conscious trials (M = .97, SD = .07), t(102) = 66.82, p<.001, BHC(0, .07 proportion correct units) = 3.78×10 82 , RRB>3 [<.001, >.5]. Both upper limits of the robustness regions were set to the maximum possible proportion, which is 0.5 units above chance. That is, strong evidence supported participants' performance being above chance for both unconscious and conscious trials.

For more detailed subliminality testing, see Appendix 2.

Attractiveness of the images. Only participants who were eligible for the analysis of the main theory were included. There were 58 heterosexual females and 34 heterosexual males. As shown in Table 4, there was strong evidence that both heterosexual males and females were subjectively attracted to the nude images of the opposite sex. Thus, this manipulation check is fully supported.

Test of the main theory. Eight participants (five heterosexual females and three heterosexual males) exceeded the pre-registered 20% breakthrough threshold and were excluded from the analysis.

The H0 for both unconscious attraction tests was modelled, considering potential conscious contamination. The observed proportion of unconscious trials (ObsUC) was .945 for heterosexual females (maximum error rate = .055). According to Dienes (2025), the maximum conscious contamination happens when error = (1-ObsUC)/2, which gave us a proposed true proportion of unconscious trials (TrueUC) of (ObsUCerror)/(1-2*error) = .971. With the parameters above, the maximum conscious contamination was error (1 -TrueUC) / ObsUC = .0008. As for heterosexual males, ObsUC = .963, TrueUC = .981, and the maximum conscious contamination was .0004 proportion correct (priming units). Using the R package "bayesplay", the respective maximum conscious contaminations were set as the upper limit of the null prior (H0 model) (see Table 5).

There was moderate evidence supporting the unconscious attraction to nude images fitting participants' sexual preferences, which was aligned with Jiang et al.'s (2006) findings. For other relevant supplementary analyses that were not registered in Stage 1, please see Appendix 2.

Discussion

We replicated various key findings of Jiang et al. (2006), but not all of them.

Contrary to Jiang et al., we established that participants were above the objective threshold in discriminating which side the nude image was on. The perception was nonetheless unconscious according to the subjective threshold. This discrepancy could result from our exclusion criteria for the manipulation check. We eliminated invalid response patterns, which consist of awareness checks (more than 20% of unconscious trials were reported with confidence) and response patterns (more than 16 consecutive identical responses in the image location discrimination task). The invalid pattern criterion excluded another 55 participants from the subliminality analysis, which showed a chance-level performance (M = .50, SD = .02), t(54) = -0.44, p = .664, BHC(0, .07 proportion correct units) = 0.018 RRB<1/3 [.003, >.50]. The inclusion of these invalid participants did not shift the above objective threshold conclusion (M = .52, SD = .08), t(157) = 3.49, p <.001, BHC(0, .07 proportion correct units) = 46.13 RRB>3 [<.001, >.50]. While a small effect, it is a non-negligible discriminative capacity. And that can be interpreted as valuable for arguing that what was unconscious (by the subjective threshold) was genuine seeing: The visual information functionally constituted the mental state of seeing, and was not just information in the neural tissue (Peters et al., 2017). The seeing was unconscious because the participants were not aware of seeing (on higher-order theories, Rosenthal, 2005). Finding priming below the subjective rather than objective threshold is typical of past subliminal priming studies, where priming below the subjective threshold is easier to obtain than below the objective (Cheesman & Merikle, 1984; Fisk & Haase, 2005; Lorentz et al., 2015).

For the manipulation check of whether heterosexual participants rated nude images of their opposite sex as attractive, there was strong evidence for H1. All heterosexual participants rated opposite-sex images as attractive (while rating the samesex images as unattractive, see appendix). This manipulation check was not employed in Jiang et al. (2006). The images are rather dated for contemporary young eyes, so it was crucial to show that the relevant images were actually attractive. It's worth noting the difference between female and male participants, as heterosexual male participants expressed around 3 times stronger attitudes toward both male and female images. This would explain the sample size difference needed for the Bayes factor to reach the stopping threshold.

For the main research question, we hypothesised that subliminal images of the opposite sex would attract heterosexual participants' attention. There was moderate evidence to support this claim, with both heterosexual male and female participants showing unconscious attentional attraction toward opposite-sex images. The important conclusion is that attention can operate without conscious awareness, as defined by a subjective threshold. While unconscious trials with breakthrough reports were removed from the analysis, a near-zero priming effect in conscious trials (see Appendix 2 for related results) makes it safe to exclude the possibility of conscious contamination. A related concern is that participants may have reported stimuli as invisible, not because of the lack of visual experience, but to comply with perceived expectations. If this were the case, nominally unconscious trials would contain a proportion of genuinely visible trials, and priming in the two conditions should converge rather than diverge. A dedicated analysis and discussion are provided in Appendix 2.

Our findings further suggest that the sex-related context of the suppressed images was a determining factor in the process. Emotionally salient stimuli have been established to break through CFS with less signal strength compared to neutral counterparts (Tsuchiya et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2014), indicating their high priority in processing subliminally. Aligning with the rationale that mating needs have cognitive significance, Hung et al. (2016) found individuals showed unconscious attentional bias toward more attractive faces through an orientation task similar to Jiang et al.'s (and ours) but used inhibition of return to define attraction.

Human faces, especially emotionally salient ones, have been shown to have advantages in both conscious and unconscious processing (Almeida et al., 2013; Eitam et al., 2014; Pegna et al., 2008; Troiani & Schultz, 2013; Yang et al., 2007; Ziori & Dienes, 2015) and in capturing attention (Di Giorgio et al., 2012; Morrisey et al., 2019; Sadr & Krowicki, 2019; Stoesz & Jakobson, 2014; Vuilleumier, 2000). On the other hand, the naked human body has been less used in consciousness science. Most et al. (2007) found female erotic images were effective distractors for both male and female participants (sexual orientation unspecified). However, no compelling evidence supported visible erotic images as viable cues for visuospatial attention (Imhoff et al., 2020; Novák et al., 2020), which aligns with our findings in the conscious condition (See Appendix 2). With the evidence at hand, it is possible that our heterosexual participants were processing and attending to the human faces, which all our nude materials had, instead of attending to the proposed naked bodies. Future studies could employ the same paradigm where just faces are presented with different levels of attractiveness or suggestive expressions, or where naked bodies are presented with obscured faces. For related exploratory tests on our current data, see Appendix 2.

The finding of attentional capture below the subjective threshold fits in with claims of unconscious working memory. Soto et al. (2011) and Soto and Silvanto (2014) challenged the conventional view of working memory contents being strictly conscious.

They proposed that working memory can be engaged without awareness and operate on subliminal representations. A recent multi-lab registered report (Franco-Martínez et al., 2026) confirmed above-chance working memory performance for stimuli reported as unseen, and found that performance was positively correlated with cue detection sensitivity. Crucially, the regression intercept remained above chance after correcting for measurement error, indicating that working memory performance was predicted to be above chance even for a hypothetical observer with zero perceptual sensitivity. This suggests that unconscious representations can enter and be maintained in working memory, even if performance also benefits from greater awareness. This framework can interpret our findings as subliminal stimuli that captured participants' attention may have been maintained in working memory below the conscious threshold. However, the debate is not settled (e.g., Stein et al., 2016), and an alternative explanation is that attention to a stimulus does not always result in its information entering working memory.

The findings bear on several theories of consciousness and raise questions about how conscious perception develops and operates (Cleeremans et al., 2020). According to attention schema theory (Graziano, 2022), conscious perception arises when one models one's attention as attending to the stimulus. The model of attention is schematic, that is, it is an imperfect representation of how attention is working; thus, attention can be drawn to stimuli without one modelling it as being so drawn (Wilterson et al., 2020).

That is the phenomenon of subliminal stimuli drawing attention, as we found in replicating Jiang et al. (2006). The attention schema theory also predicts that one can implicitly learn to attend in certain ways guided by subliminal stimuli if the contingencies are repeated often enough, a prediction confirmed by Wilterson et al., providing a different sort of evidence for subliminal stimuli guiding attention. Relevant to our findings, the theory allows that distractors are less distracting if they are conscious rather than unconscious; that is, because if the distractors are conscious, attention to those distractors is being modelled, and because attention is being modelled, it can be suitably controlled. (Note: although Wilterson et al. made the argument of the last sentence, the theory also allows conscious distractors to be more distracting than unconscious ones: If the distractors are conscious, that is because they are being attended, and the more attended they are, the more distracting they will be.) The theory thus allows for a viable explanation of the conscious images that do not produce priming (as we found, see Appendix 2, replicating Jiang et al.): Attention was not drawn to them because it was being successfully modelled. However, the lack of priming with conscious cues we found could also be explained by attention being drawn to the nude images more quickly and then quickly returned to the centre. This may result in the inhibition of return, although we did not find inhibitory priming. Future studies using different durations of primes and delays in the Gabor patch task, as well as implementing other attention study measures (e.g., eye tracking), could address this question.

Attention schema theory claims perception is conscious when one represents that one is attending. Higher order theories (e.g. Rosenthal, 2018) make a more general claim: A mental state is conscious when one represents in a suitable way that one is in that mental state. Representing that one is attending is to consciously attend; but representing one is seeing is to consciously see; one experiences the conscious seeing as specifically seeing. A core intuition is that unconscious perceptual states occur when the world appears in a certain way (the way the world is unconsciously represented as being); conscious mental states are those mental states appearing in a certain way (the way the mental states are represented as being). Such an approach justifies using a subjective threshold to indicate subliminality (subjective measures measure whether one represents oneself as being in a mental state). Higher order theories also allow attending to the naked images without being aware of so attending, that is, they allow attention to be drawn to subliminal images. Lamme (2004) presents a first-order theory of a visual state being conscious: The state is conscious if there is a cortical recurrence, which does not necessarily enable reports of the experience. Questions about where conscious perception ends and higherlevel cognition begins remain actively debated (Block, 2023). On this theory, when our participants denied seeing the image, the seeing could still have been conscious. This theory does not motivate subjective measures, but it could take being above the objective threshold as evidence for recurrence (by way of indicating a representation stable enough to control behaviour), and hence awareness. On this account, our study did not establish that the seeing was subliminal. That is, on this theory, attention may be guided by phenomenally conscious images.

Another first-order theory is the global workspace theory (Baars, 1993; Mashour et al., 2020). On this theory, seeing is conscious if the information enters a global workspace by way of attention. Further, once information is in the global workspace, it would be available to whatever mechanism produces higher-order states (representations of being in a mental state); thus, subjective measures are justified as measures of whether a mental state is conscious. While the subliminal attraction of attention may seem to falsify the theory, Mashour et al, commenting on studies like Jiang et al (2006), said "It should be recognized that what we call "attention" is actually a diverse set of temporal, spatial, and cognitive filters; thus, many of these filters may operate non-consciously, with only the final one gating entry in the global workspace." (Mashour et al., 2020, pp. 783) Thus, this explanation contrasts with the one that information entered working memory unconsciously; rather, it did not enter at all. Our paradigm does not provide evidence to discriminate between these accounts. However, using CFS to test unconscious working memory is not a novel idea, with studies showing encouraging evidence that supports the operation and retention of unconscious working memory (Bergström & Eriksson, 2015; Pan et al., 2014; Song & Yao, 2016), with neuronal evidence that such information could last as long as 15 seconds (Bergström & Eriksson, 2018).

By adding a variety of waiting times (or even distractors) before the identification task, as well as manipulating the content of suppressed stimuli in the current paradigm, we should be able to provide robust evidence on unconscious memory, and whether the salience of emotional stimuli helps with its retention.

There are a few crucial procedural details to bear in mind for any future replications. Firstly, there are wide individual differences in the performance on the Gabor patch identification task. The main study employed a staircase procedure to ensure that performance on the Gabor patches was roughly in the middle of the range, thereby ruling out floor or ceiling effects. Mean performance on the pilot was .83 (SD = .12), which may have made an increase in performance due to priming hard to detect; in the main study, in which difficulty was titrated for each participant, the performance was .68 (SD = .10) among participants eligible for analysis.

Secondly, the priming material presented in Jiang et al.'s (2006) diagram caused consistent breakthroughs during the pilot; thus, for the main study, we adjusted the images' colour scale and contrast to make them less salient. After the adjustment, suppression became stable for the main experiment. We advise future replication attempts to take these adjustments into account. Throughout this paper, we use "unconscious" and "subliminal" interchangeably to refer to stimuli and mental processes below the threshold of consciousness, as it suits the framework we were working with; for a more detailed discussion of theoretical distinctions between these terms, see Tsikandilakis et al. (2026).

An open question is the extent to which different methods for rendering stimuli subliminal, other than CFS, are able to produce subliminal capture of attention with the same paradigm. An advantage of trying different methods is that they may produce stronger or weaker effects, or show whether attention can be captured by material at the objective threshold. We have studies in progress addressing this question. One promising candidate will be visual masking. Validated for achieving suppression at both subjective and objective thresholds (Breitmeyer & Öğmen, 2006; Kouider & Dehaene, 2007), visual masking disrupts processing through temporal interference, potentially allowing for more precise control over the depth of suppression (Enns & Di Lollo, 2000). While CFS allows longer exposure of subliminal visual stimuli, visual masking, in theory, should provide a cleaner dissociation between unconscious processing and conscious access, as the feedforward signal is relatively intact and only the recurrent processing is disrupted (Lamme & Roelfsema, 2000; Wyatte et al., 2012).

Previous work has demonstrated that visual stimuli can be processed under visual masking, eliciting attention shifts (Carlson & Reinke, 2008; Kentridge et al., 2008).

Masked emotionally salient content can be subliminally processed (Morris et al., 1998; Whalen et al., 1998). Ever since Marcel's (1983) work on subliminal perception, visual masking has remained one of the main approaches in unconscious processing research.

While the evidence in comparing the effectiveness of CFS and visual masking is conflicting (Faivre et al., 2012; Izatt et al., 2014; Almeida et al., 2008; Almeida et al., 2013), the difference in their core mechanism suggests an interesting research direction.

In conclusion, with reasonable adjustments to the original design, we replicated Jiang et al. (2006) specifically with respect to the unconscious attraction toward opposite-sex nude images among heterosexual individuals, given the subliminality established by the subjective threshold. Our results suggested that participants retained spatial knowledge of the suppressed images enough to perform above chance when instructed to make a 2AFC. These findings support the arguments that attention and consciousness are dissociable, and that our brain can subliminally process emotionally salient stimuli such as erotic nude images.

A Bayes factor >3 indicates evidence for H1, while a B<1/3 indicates evidence for H0. We showed we will be able to recruit enough participants to achieve at least this level of evidence.

If the evidence for unconscious trials supports H0, we will conclude that the CFS effectively rendered conscious knowledge unconscious; if B > 3, we will conclude that perception was above objective threshold; if B is between these ranges we will draw no conclusions regarding objective threshold. However, as we discard trials when the participant said they saw, if performance is above objective threshold, we will still conclude that perception was below subjective threshold.

If the evidence for conscious trials supports H1, we can conclude that the participants were above objective threshold for discriminating the nude location during trials; if the evidence supports H0, then the participants could not consciously perceive experiment stimuli. The model of H0 will be a uniform from 0 to max, where max is defined as per Dienes (2022).

A Bayes factor >3 indicates good evidence for H1, while a B<1/3 suggests good evidence for H0. We have shown we can collect enough participants to reach at this level of evidence.

We will draw conclusions for each participant sex separately. If the results support H1, then subliminal naked images of the opposite sex are able to attract attention. If the results support H0, then subliminal naked images of the opposite sex are not able to attract attention.

It is worth noting that the sample size of homosexual individuals, male or female, was inadequate, not allowing for clear conclusions in general. Jiang et al. (2006) did recruit non-heterosexual participants. However, bisexuals and homosexuals were grouped as one; their sexual preferences are nonetheless different. We encourage future studies to investigate the question with a more dedicated sample and design (including appropriate stimuli selected for attractiveness for the relevant population).

Split-half reliability.

To test the reliability of the paradigm in measuring individual differences, the unconscious trials for heterosexual participants observing opposite sex images were split in half. The correlation between attention effects from the first and second halves of the trials was -.208, 95% CI [-.396, -.003]. Jiang et al. (2006) did not report a reliability. A very similar task, the dot-probe task, also has low reliability. Xu et al. (2025), in an extensive study on 9,600 participants across 36 variations of a dotprobe task with emotional faces, found the split-half reliability to average 0. That is, the Jiang et al. task, as the dot-probe task, is not appropriate for studying individual differences without dramatically increasing the number of trials. Reassuringly, with the numbers of trials used, the task could not be used to surreptitiously measure sexuality of an individual. Nonetheless, the tasks are suitable for measuring group effects, as we have demonstrated (cf. Hedge et al., 2018; Schuch et al., 2022).

Gender differentiation.

To test if the participants could process the sex of the invisible images undergoing CFS, we grouped both the heterosexual males and females into a single "heterosexual group" and then compared the difference in attention effects between invisible opposite-sex images and same-sex images.

pattern also counts against the regression-to-the-mean account. If unconscious priming were an artefact of conscious trials being mislabelled as unconscious, the unconscious effect should be smaller than the conscious one. Priming present only in the unconscious condition is the opposite of what contamination predicts (Dienes, 2025; Skora et al., 2023). For similar reasons, the divergence between conditions is hard to reconcile with demand-driven misreporting of visibility. If participants were calling visible trials invisible to comply with perceived expectations, we should observe similar results in the two conditions.

Additional attentional effects.

One of the key findings of Jiang et al. (2006), besides the registered unconscious attraction towards nude images that fit individuals' sexual preferences, was the repelling effect of images that do not. The repulsion effect was most prevalent in heterosexual male participants toward male nude images.

However, in our replication, there was moderate to strong evidence supporting the H0 for the proposed unconscious repelling effect for same-sex nude images among heterosexual participants. As for the conscious priming effect from nude images, there was moderate to strong evidence for H0, supporting Jiang et al.'s claims that such priming only prevails in subliminal processing (see Table 8). These findings are considered in the main discussion.

Table 8 Attentional shift (difference in proportion correct) toward nude images for participants in the main CFS experiment. Positive values indicate attentional attraction. The upper limit of the robustness region was set to the maximum effect size, which is 1.0 of the difference in proportion correct. *= expected negative values

The lack of attentional repulsion from same-sex images among heterosexual participants could be explained by participants' overall positive attitudes towards nonheterosexual orientations. However, we cannot make a direct comparison since personal attitudes were not the focus of Jiang et al. (2006). Our findings should serve as an anchor for future studies, where the subliminal attentional effects can be compared between high and low-homophobic individuals. Another potential explanation for the absence of repulsion is the greater exposure to sexually explicit images on the internet among younger generations, which may promote an increase in openness to diverse sexual orientations (Owens et al., 2012; Wéry & Billieux, 2017). According to the House of Commons Education Committee (2024), UK adolescents spent five hours on their mobile devices and computers daily before COVID-19, which likely increased further during the pandemic (Trott et al., 2022). Considering Jiang et al. was conducted before the first appearance of smartphones, the substantially different experience with the internet could have resulted in the elimination of aversive responses toward samesex nude images, especially among males who are presumed to consume sexual content (e.g., pornography or sexually suggestive media) more frequently than females (Ballester-Arnal et al., 2023). This assumption, while requiring further investigation, opens a new line of research on the influence of the internet, such as potentially desensitising individuals to graphic stimuli (with the possible positive outcome amongst some of greater mindfulness of the body). There was not enough good evidence that heterosexual participants could discriminate the sex of the nude images when being suppressed by CFS. A growing body of literature suggests CFS operates through feature-selective suppression mechanisms that preferentially target stimuli based on spatial frequency, temporal frequency, luminance, and contrast, instead of higher-level content such as sexual information (Han et al., 2016; Stein et al., 2014). Moors et al. (2017) further proposed that CFS does not rely on visual integration to suppress perception. Instead, CFS fractures the visual representations into elementary visual properties. In other words, under CFS individuals could be unconsciously responding to body outlines and edge contrast of the intact nude images, rather than the semantic categorisation of biological sex. The theory that CFS involves minimal processing would be consistent with attraction not being specifically to bodies of the opposite sex, but to any meaningful structure (contrast the repulsion effect in Jiang et al., 2006). But we do not yet know; more participants are needed. Note the robustness region indicates there would be evidence for H1 using a scale factor between .011 and .07 proportion correct units. The observed effect sizes from the main attention priming toward preferred stimuli averaged at .04 proportion correct units. If we had used a basic effect heuristic of Dienes (2019), i.e. a SD = .04 for the test of priming being different between genders, the Bayes factor BHN(0, .037 proportion correct units) = 4.18. As this is a reasonable, though post hoc argument, no conclusion is robust at this stage. Supporting the claim that subliminal perception includes the gender of the naked body, a study we completed (manuscript in preparation), essentially the same as the current study except for using backwards masking rather than CFS, revealed evidence for a difference in attentional attraction to preferred versus non-preferred genders using the unadjusted H1 SD of .10.

Group differentiation.

To validate the main attention effect, we compared the difference between heterosexual and homosexual (which are the two sexual orientations with expected distinctive preference towards male and female nude images) participants, as well as between unconscious and conscious trials. In respect of the individuality of each sexual orientation, four comparisons of attention effect were made between heterosexual and homosexual males and females, towards male and female images, with SE calculated as the √(SEhetero 2 + SEhomo 2 ). There was moderate evidence supporting H0 for no performance difference between heterosexual and homosexual females, while inconclusive for male participants (see Table 12).

For the comparison between heterosexual and homosexual males, since there were only two homosexual male participants, the inconclusive result was expected. As for the comparison in female participants, homosexual female participants, against the expectation, presented an unconscious attraction effect towards male images, which explains the evidence for H0 in both individual attention effect analysis and in comparison, to heterosexual females. More robust evidence is needed to make a decision on whether heterosexual and homosexual individuals respond differently to invisible nude images.

As for the comparison between unconscious and conscious trials, all heterosexual participants were grouped together, and the attention effect towards opposite-sex images was compared between conscious and unconscious trials. There was moderate evidence for H1 that heterosexual participants performed differently in the attention task between unconscious and conscious trials (see Table 13).

There is a distinction between one's attention being drawn to a naked body before one is consciously aware of the body; and one's attention being drawn without one ever being consciously aware of the stimulus. Jiang et al. appear to establish the latter stronger case. The strong attentional priming effect at the objective threshold from Jiang et al. is a crucial piece of evidence for the ongoing debate between attention and consciousness, and thus in need of a pre-registered replication.

(2006) defined the attentional effects as the difference in proportion correct between the aligned (Gabor patches appeared on the same side as the intact nude images) and not-aligned (Gabor patches appeared on the opposite side to the intact nude images) conditions.

Thus, a positive score indicates attentional attraction, and a negative score indicates repulsion. The attentional effects for each gender×sexual orientation group were not precisely specified in Jiang et al. but generally lay around 0.1 (difference in proportion correct) on graphs for unconscious trials. In contrast, the conscious trials .

Figure 1 )

If unconscious attention is based on low frequency information, a body outline may be what is drawing attention, not the internal high frequency details. Thus, for the main study we will scramble the rectangle containing the image, as Jiang et al. did, so low frequency information cannot draw attention to the scrambled image (see Figure2).

) = 3.78, p < .001, BHC(0, .07 proportion correct units) = 125 RRB>3 [<.001, >.5]. Consistent with the whole experiment sample, there was strong evidence for H1 that the performance was abovechance for heterosexual participants discriminating intact nude image locations under CFS, even with reports of no visual experience.To see whether the consecutive pattern exclusion worked as designed, we analysed the difference in RT between invalid consecutive and non-consecutive pattern responses. The H1 model is a half-normal, with the prior set to half the maximum difference, which is the RT for non-consecutive pattern responses (M = 1.23 sec). The mean difference in RT was M = 0.67 sec, SD = 0.83, t(54) = 6.04, p < .001, BHN(0, 0.61 sec) = 2.92*10 5 RRB>3 [0.03, >1.23]. There was strong evidence of a decrease in RT between consecutive patterned and normal responses among excluded participants, suggesting that participants may have lost engagement with the image-location discrimination task.
